title: Architecture Decisions Are Bets: A Senior Engineer’s Playbook for Choosing the Right Trade-offs
partialText:
One framework, six real-world dilemmas, and the hidden costs most teams miss

Every architecture decision is a bet.

You are betting that your traffic will grow a certain way. That your team will stay a certain size. That a vendor will still exist in three years. That the “temporary” fix will actually be temporary.

Junior engineers look for the right answer. Senior engineers know there usually isn’t one. There is only the best bet for this team, with these constraints, at this moment — and a plan for what to do if the bet goes wrong.

In this post, I’ll share the framework I use to make those bets, walk through six dilemmas that show up in almost every growing system, and point out the second-order costs that usually get ignored until production finds them for you.

Step 0: Frame the Problem Before You Touch the Whiteboard

Most bad architecture isn’t caused by picking the wrong technology. It’s caused by solving the wrong problem. Before I compare options, I answer five questions:

  1. What problem are we actually solving? When someone says “we need microservices,” I keep asking why until I hit the real driver. It’s usually one of three things: deploy speed, team autonomy, or scaling one specific hot path. Each of those has a different (and often cheaper) solution.
  2. What are the hard constraints? Latency budget, peak throughput, budget, compliance (GDPR, HIPAA, PCI), and — the one everybody forgets — the skills of the team that will be on call for this at 3 a.m.
  3. What are the quality attributes, ranked? You can’t maximize availability, consistency, cost, and simplicity all at once. Force a ranking. “Correctness over latency” is a decision; “everything matters” is not.
  4. What does success look like in numbers? “Fast” is not a requirement. “p99 under 200 ms at 5,000 requests per second” is.
  5. Who else is affected? Product, ops, security, finance. They surface constraints you’d never find in the code.

Then I write it all on one page. If I can’t explain the problem and constraints on a single page, I don’t understand it well enough to design for it.

The Framework: Reversibility × Blast Radius

Not every decision deserves the same amount of debate. The most useful filter I know is to score each decision on two axes:

  • Reversibility: How expensive is it to undo this in a year? Swapping a logging library is cheap. Migrating your primary database is a multi-quarter project.
  • Blast radius: If we’re wrong, how much breaks? One service, or the whole company?

This gives you four zones:

  • Easy to reverse, small blast radius → Just decide. Let the team that owns it pick, and move on. Debating these is the most common waste of senior engineering time.
  • Easy to reverse, large blast radius → Experiment. Use feature flags, canaries, and gradual rollouts. Let data decide.
  • Hard to reverse, small blast radius → Contain it. Put it behind an interface so that if it’s wrong, the damage stays local.
  • Hard to reverse, large blast radius → Slow down. Prototype, write an ADR, get reviews. This is where your seniority actually earns its keep.

Amazon calls this one-way vs. two-way doors. The key insight is that a lot of seemingly one-way decisions can be turned into two-way decisions with a bit of upfront design — an abstraction layer, a migration path, a vendor-neutral API. Making decisions reversible is often more valuable than making them correct.

Now let’s put the framework to work.

Dilemma 1: Synchronous APIs vs. Event-Driven Communication

The scenario: You run an online store. When a payment succeeds, the order service must start fulfillment and the inventory service must deduct stock. Flash sales push traffic 20× above normal.

Option A: The payment service calls the order and inventory services directly over REST.
Option B: The payment service publishes a PaymentConfirmed event to Kafka, and downstream services consume it independently.

With synchronous calls, the payment service’s latency becomes the sum of its dependencies, and its availability becomes the product of theirs. Three services at 99.9% each give you roughly 99.7% for the whole chain. During a flash sale, one slow inventory query backs up threads in the payment service, and suddenly customers can’t pay at all.

With events, the payment service does one thing — record the payment and publish a fact — and returns. Each consumer scales on its own, fails on its own, and catches up on its own. Want to add email receipts, analytics, or loyalty points later? Subscribe to the same event. Zero changes to payment.

My call: Event-driven for this flow. But here’s what most articles leave out — the three things you must get right, or events will hurt you more than REST ever did:

  1. The dual-write problem. If you write the payment to your database and then publish to Kafka, a crash in between leaves you with a payment that no one ever fulfills. Use the transactional outbox pattern: write the event to an outbox table in the same transaction as the payment, and have a relay (or CDC tool like Debezium) publish it.
  2. Idempotent consumers. Kafka gives you at-least-once delivery in practice. Your inventory service will see the same event twice. Track processed event IDs, or make the operation naturally idempotent.
  3. Observability. A request that used to be one stack trace is now spread across three services and a broker. Propagate correlation IDs and monitor consumer lag from day one.

And notice what stays synchronous: the payment itself. The customer needs an immediate yes or no. The rule I use is simple — synchronous for what the user is waiting on, asynchronous for everything that happens because of it.

Dilemma 2: Build vs. Buy

The scenario: You’re launching an enterprise mobile app that needs MFA, biometric login, SSO with corporate identity providers, and compliance with GDPR and HIPAA.

Option A: Build authentication in-house.
Option B: Use a managed identity provider (Auth0, Okta, AWS Cognito, Azure AD B2C).

My call: Buy. But the reason matters more than the answer.

The question I ask is: is this our core, or our context? Core is what makes customers choose you. Context is everything you need to do well but that no customer will ever pay extra for. Authentication is context for almost everyone. Getting it slightly wrong is catastrophic; getting it perfectly right earns you nothing extra.

Buying isn’t free, though. Before signing, I check three things:

  • Total cost at 10× scale. Per-monthly-active-user pricing that looks cheap at 10,000 users can be painful at 1,000,000.
  • The exit strategy. Can you export user records and password hashes? Hide the vendor behind your own thin auth interface so switching is a contained migration, not a rewrite. This turns a one-way door into a two-way door.
  • Customization limits. Find out before you commit which flows the vendor can’t support.

Build when the capability is your differentiator, when no vendor meets a hard constraint, or when you’ve outgrown the vendor and have the team to own it forever. “Forever” is the important word — you’re not building a feature, you’re adopting a product.

Dilemma 3: Monolith vs. Microservices

The scenario: A startup is building a SaaS platform with user management, billing, and notifications. It hasn’t found product-market fit yet. Speed matters most.

My call: A modular monolith. This one isn’t close.

Microservices solve an organizational problem: letting many teams deploy independently without stepping on each other. If you have one or two teams, you don’t have that problem yet — but you will pay all of the costs: network failures, distributed transactions, versioned APIs, a dozen deployment pipelines, and debugging across process boundaries.

The word that does the heavy lifting is modular. A modular monolith means:

  • Clear module boundaries aligned to business domains (billing, identity, notifications).
  • Modules talk through public interfaces, never by reaching into each other’s tables.
  • Those rules are enforced by tooling (ArchUnit, import linters, module systems), not by good intentions.

Then you extract a service only when a concrete trigger shows up: one module needs to scale very differently from the rest, a team is constantly blocked on another team’s deploys, or a module needs a different tech stack or isolation for compliance. Shopify still runs one of the largest Rails monoliths in the world — modularized, not split.

Dilemma 4: SQL vs. NoSQL for Flexible Data

The scenario: You’re building a CRM where each customer can add custom fields to contacts — industry, revenue, priority. The system is expected to grow quickly.

A lot of people jump to “flexible schema = NoSQL.” I think that’s usually the wrong instinct.

My call: PostgreSQL, with fixed columns for the core fields and a JSONB column for custom fields, indexed with a GIN index.

Here’s why:

  • CRMs are query-heavy. Sales teams filter, segment, join contacts to companies and deals, and run reports. That’s exactly what relational databases are great at, and exactly where document stores make you work hard.
  • JSONB gives you most of the flexibility. You can store arbitrary custom fields, index them, and query them, while keeping transactions and constraints for the core data.
  • “NoSQL scales better” is mostly outdated. A well-tuned Postgres instance handles far more load than most CRMs will ever see, and read replicas, partitioning, and tools like Citus take you much further.

When would I choose a NoSQL store like DynamoDB or MongoDB? When access patterns are simple and known in advance (fetch by key, small range queries), when scale is massive and predictable, or when the data is truly document-shaped and rarely joined. The real question isn’t “SQL or NoSQL?” — it’s “what are my access patterns, and which store serves them with the least effort?”

Dilemma 5: Cache Now vs. Precompute Later

The scenario: Your streaming platform’s recommendation query is indexed and well written, but at peak it takes 2 seconds and hammers the database. Customers are complaining, and leadership wants a fix this week.

Option A: Add a Redis cache in front of the query.
Option B: Build an async pipeline that precomputes recommendations and serves them from a read-optimized store.

My call: Cache now, precompute next. These aren’t competing options; they’re two stages of the same plan.

A cache-aside layer can ship in days and typically cuts repeat queries from seconds to single-digit milliseconds. But caches come with their own failure modes, and senior engineers plan for them up front:

  • Cache stampede. When a popular key expires, thousands of requests miss at once and all hit the database. Use request coalescing (one fetch per key) or refresh-ahead before expiry.
  • TTL jitter. If every key expires at exactly 10 minutes, they’ll all expire together. Add randomness.
  • Staleness budget. Agree with product on how stale recommendations can be. For recommendations, minutes are fine. For account balances, they aren’t.
  • Cold start. After a deploy or a Redis failover, your hit rate is zero. Make sure the database can survive that moment, or pre-warm the cache.

Once the fire is out, move to precomputation: a batch or streaming job generates recommendations per user and writes them to a key-value store. Reads become a single lookup, and load becomes predictable. My rule: cache for quick wins, precompute for predictable load, and never let a quick win become the permanent architecture by accident.

Dilemma 6: Rewrite vs. Refactor

The scenario: You inherit a 20-year-old monolith. It runs the business. It’s full of tech debt. Developers are afraid to touch it.

Option A: Start fresh with a clean rewrite.
Option B: Modernize it incrementally.

My call: Incremental — specifically, the Strangler Fig pattern.

Big rewrites fail for a predictable reason: the old system is a decade of undocumented business rules, and the new one has to rediscover every one of them while the business keeps changing the target. Meanwhile, you’re shipping nothing new.

The Strangler Fig works like this:

  1. Put a routing layer in front (an API gateway or proxy). All traffic goes through it.
  2. Add characterization tests around the area you’re about to change, so you capture what the system actually does, not what the docs say.
  3. Carve out one capability at a time — start with something low-risk and high-value — and route its traffic to the new implementation.
  4. Run old and new side by side where you can (shadow traffic, comparing outputs) before cutting over.
  5. Repeat until the legacy core is small enough to retire, or stable enough to leave alone.

Every step ships. Every step is reversible — just flip the route back. That’s the framework again: you’ve turned one giant one-way door into dozens of two-way doors.

Write It Down: The Architecture Decision Record

The decision is only half the work. The other half is making sure that in 18 months, someone (probably you) understands why. That’s what an Architecture Decision Record (ADR) is for. Mine fit on one page:

ADR-042: Use events for post-payment workflows

Status: Accepted (2026-11-16)
Context: Flash sales cause payment failures when inventory
         is slow. Payment availability is our top priority.
Options: (A) Sync REST chain  (B) Kafka events + outbox
Decision: (B). Payment stays sync; fulfillment and
          inventory consume PaymentConfirmed.
Consequences: + Isolation, independent scaling
              - Eventual consistency, need idempotency
Revisit if: Consumer lag > 5 min, or ordering needs
            span multiple aggregates.

The most underrated line is “Revisit if.” It turns a decision into a hypothesis with an expiry condition, so nobody has to argue later about whether it’s time to reconsider.

Seven Mistakes I See Even Experienced Engineers Make

  1. Resume-driven design. Choosing the tech you want to learn instead of the tech the problem needs.
  2. Designing for imaginary scale. Building for 100 million users when you have 1,000 — and missing the product deadline as a result.
  3. Ignoring operational cost. Every new component is something to monitor, patch, upgrade, and wake up for.
  4. Treating every decision as a one-way door. Spending weeks debating what could be undone in an afternoon.
  5. Treating one-way doors casually. Picking a primary database in a 15-minute meeting.
  6. Skipping the prototype. A two-day spike beats two weeks of whiteboard arguments about performance.
  7. Not writing it down. Decisions without recorded context get reversed by the next person for the wrong reasons.

Want to Get Better at This, Faster?

Good judgment comes from experience — but you don’t have to get all of that experience the hard way. Studying how real systems were designed, and why, is the fastest shortcut I know. That’s exactly why we built the courses at DesignGurus.io:

  • Grokking System Design Fundamentals — caching, databases, replication, partitioning, and messaging: the building blocks behind every trade-off in this post.
  • Grokking Modern Software Architecture Styles — monoliths, modular monoliths, microservices, event-driven and more, with when (and when not) to use each.
  • Grokking Kafka and Event-Driven Architecture — outbox, idempotency, consumer groups, and everything you need to make Dilemma 1 work in production.
  • Grokking the System Design Interview — practice making and defending these decisions end to end, the same way you’ll be asked to in senior and staff interviews.

The Takeaway

Great architects aren’t the ones who are always right. They’re the ones who:

  • Frame the problem before picking a solution.
  • Spend their energy on the decisions that are hard to undo.
  • Turn one-way doors into two-way doors wherever they can.
  • Plan for the second-order costs — the outbox, the stampede, the exit strategy.
  • Write down not just what they decided, but when to decide again.

Make your bets deliberately, hedge them wisely, and stay willing to change your mind when the data tells you to.

What’s the hardest architecture trade-off you’ve had to make? I’d love to hear about it in the comments.

Architecture Decisions Are Bets: A Senior Engineer’s Playbook for Choosing the Right Trade-offs was originally published in Level Up Coding on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: The Hidden TCO Trap of Cryptographic Capability Attenuation via Ephemeral Token Proof-of-Possession…
partialText:
The Hidden TCO Trap of Cryptographic Capability Attenuation via Ephemeral Token Proof-of-Possession (AI Governance fiduciary liability): Beyond Token Pricing

Why infrastructure overhead, cold starts, and evaluations dwarf raw model API costs

Visualizing the hidden architectural and compute overhead of cryptographic capability attenuation in autonomous systems.

📊 Executive Summary: While executives obsess over LLM API token costs, the true margin killer in regulated agentic AI is cryptographic authorization overhead. Implementing ephemeral Proof-of-Possession and capability attenuation to satisfy fiduciary AI governance introduces severe cold-start latencies that effortlessly dwarf raw inference costs, demanding a fundamental infrastructure re-architecture.

The Latency Death Spiral: When Autonomous Agents Meet Fiduciary Proof-of-Possession

At precisely 09:00 UTC on a Tuesday, a Tier-1 global bank initiated the production deployment of a sovereign, multi-hop agentic workflow engineered to automate cross-border commercial loan origination. The core Large Language Model (LLM) API was flawlessly optimized, processing high-complexity credit analyses at a raw inference cost of roughly $0.04 per transaction. Yet, within twenty minutes of ingesting live traffic, the deployment triggered a cascading latency death spiral that shattered the designated service-level agreements. The failure had nothing to do with the neural network’s prompt processing or output generation. Instead, the architecture collapsed under its own security weight because every autonomous sub-agent in the workflow was strictly mandated to mint, attest, and verify ephemeral Proof-of-Possession (PoP) keys for every outbound request to satisfy boardroom-mandated zero-trust boundaries (Fett et al., 2023; Prakash, 2026). In an attempt to comply with RFC 9449 standardizing Demonstrating Proof-of-Possession (DPoP), the orchestration layer required each agent hop to negotiate asymmetric cryptographic signatures in real-time, effectively paralyzing the data pipeline.

The financial post-mortem of this deployment revealed a devastating unit economic reality that offshore IT integrators fundamentally missed during sandbox testing. The actual cost of operating the autonomous workflow was not the heavily negotiated LLM token pricing, but rather the crushing infrastructure overhead of the authorization mechanism itself. As leading identity providers noted in late 2026, forcing high-throughput resource APIs to execute per-request asymmetric cryptographic verification for DPoP introduces massive compute overhead at the API Gateway layer (Fett et al., 2023). Because the bank’s legacy deployment relied on serverless cloud functions to evaluate these cryptographic capabilities on-the-fly, every discrete API call suffered severe cold starts and key generation cycles. This execution penalty spiked the compute Cost of Goods Sold (COGS) from the anticipated $0.04 to an unsustainable $1.20 per transaction. The gross margin of the enterprise AI product was entirely obliterated by the overhead of mathematically proving that the agent actually possessed the authority to execute its delegated tasks.

Fresh empirical telemetry from production incident analyses highlights the exact dimensions of this architectural bottleneck. Standard cold-path validation latencies for asymmetric DPoP signatures routinely hit 32.7ms per evaluation in serverless environments. In a basic conversational chat interface, a 30-millisecond delay is imperceptible to a human user. However, in an autonomous multi-hop agent chain executing 50 sequential steps to compile a syndicated loan packet, that delay compounds aggressively. The agent spends more time waiting for the infrastructure to decrypt, validate, and evaluate its cryptographic payload than it spends generating intelligence. This transforms the promise of agentic velocity into an insurmountable financial and operational trap.

Datalog Cold Starts and the Math of Cryptographic Attenuation

The structural mechanism driving this failure stems from the inherent inability of legacy Identity and Access Management (IAM) systems to govern machine autonomy. Traditional, centralized OAuth and JSON Web Token (JWT) architectures were designed for human users interacting with static web applications, relying on long-lived access tokens evaluated at a central authorization server. Attempting to govern an autonomous AI agent by passing a static, highly privileged JWT directly to the model exposes the enterprise to extreme Context-Stuffed Privilege Escalation. When architects attempt to restrict an agent’s permissions by simply stuffing behavioral rules into the LLM’s prompt window, they practically guarantee a security breach. An external prompt injection attack can effortlessly manipulate the LLM’s context, commanding the model to ignore its written rules and misuse the underlying static token to exfiltrate data.

The fatal cascading delays introduced by continuous cryptographic authorization checks in high-speed autonomous workflows.

To physically decouple permissioning from the vulnerable context window, heavily regulated enterprises employ Cryptographic Capability Attenuation using offline-verifiable tokens such as asymmetric Biscuits or symmetric Macaroons. This architecture enforces monotonic privilege reduction natively within the token payload itself. Rather than querying a central database, a parent agent mints a highly restricted capability token for its sub-agent, embedding complex Datalog policies directly into the token’s cryptographic structure. Each subsequent sub-agent in the delegation chain can only attenuate, or further restrict, its inherited permissions before passing the token forward. This ensures mathematically that no matter how severely the LLM’s prompt is hijacked, the token itself cannot authorize an action broader than its strictly attenuated boundaries.

🛡️ Executive Risk Calculus & SLA Alert: Under the 2025–2026 OWASP LLM06 (Excessive Agency) framework (OWASP Foundation, 2026), deploying autonomous multi-hop agents with static, over-privileged access tokens is a severe fiduciary breach. Failure to physically decouple authorization from the LLM context window exposes the enterprise to catastrophic Context-Stuffed Privilege Escalation and direct regulatory liability under the EU AI Act and DORA.

The hidden Total Cost of Ownership (TCO) trap lies in the exact engineering mechanics required to validate these attenuated capabilities. Evaluating embedded Datalog policies requires non-trivial compute resources at the API edge. When enterprises deploy this verification logic via traditional serverless architectures like AWS Lambda, the asymmetric cryptography required to validate nested Biscuit tokens triggers profound infrastructure cold starts. Furthermore, because each attenuation step appends a new signature and policy block, the payload size bloats linearly — adding roughly 340 to 380 bytes per delegation block as the agent delegates deeper sub-tasks (Prakash, 2026). This acts as a severe hidden tax on every multi-agent interaction, consuming compute cycles, memory, and bandwidth well before the API payload ever reaches the execution environment.

Mathematically isolating permissions through deeply nested, offline-verifiable capability tokens.

Operational Metric Legacy Static JWT Architecture Ephemeral Capability Tokens (Biscuits/Macaroons) Inference Latency Impact Marginal (~2ms), relies on central database caching. High cold-start penalty (≥32.7ms) due to local policy evaluation. Proof-of-Possession Overhead None; tokens are vulnerable to simple interception and replay. High; demands asymmetric signature generation per API request (RFC 9449). Payload Size & Bloat Static, minimal header footprint. 340–380 bytes per delegation block; payloads expand as rules nest. Security Posture Vulnerable to Context-Stuffed Privilege Escalation. Mathematically secure; prompt injections cannot elevate attenuated privileges. TCO / Compute Cost Low infrastructure overhead, high breach liability. Severe API gateway compute overhead, dwarfing raw LLM token costs.

Dissecting the operational impact of this transition, the compute overhead required to secure the agent chain fundamentally redefines the system’s economic viability. The transition to capability tokens mathematically eradicates excessive agency vulnerabilities, but it demands an order of magnitude more CPU cycles at the network perimeter. The table above illustrates how the introduction of offline verifiable capabilities fundamentally shifts the engineering burden from the authorization database to the API gateway, forcing organizations to pay a premium in compute COGS to secure autonomous execution environments.

Fiduciary Liability in the Age of Agentic DORA and SEC Mandates

Confronted with the crushing compute overhead of capability attenuation, executive leadership frequently asks a dangerous strategic question: why not simply bypass this cryptographic complexity and rely on traditional static tokens wrapped in heavier network firewalls? The answer lies in the non-negotiable statutory reality of 2026. Deploying autonomous, multi-hop agents with static, over-privileged access tokens is no longer merely a poor architectural decision; it is a boardroom-level compliance breach. Regulatory frameworks such as the European Union AI Act, the Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA), and recent stringent United States Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) mandates explicitly require systemic risk containment for automated decision systems. Failing to enforce granular, cryptographic boundaries on an AI agent’s authority directly violates fiduciary duties surrounding corporate risk management.

Navigating the precarious equilibrium of regulatory compliance, board liability, and agentic autonomy.

The balance-sheet blast radius of failing to implement capability attenuation is staggering. If a context-stuffed privilege escalation attack tricks a multi-hop financial agent into executing unauthorized corporate fund transfers, or manipulates a healthcare agent into exfiltrating sovereign patient records, the ensuing liability easily exceeds tens of millions of dollars in statutory fines and class-action damages. Under current 2026 interpretations of excessive agency (OWASP LLM06) (OWASP Foundation, 2026), the legal liability for such an event rests squarely on the shoulders of the C-suite for failing to implement the “minimum necessary” cryptographic constraints (IAMDevBox, 2026; NHI Management Group, 2026; Veski et al., 2026). The deployment of ephemeral Demonstrating Proof-of-Possession (DPoP) and dynamic capability attenuation is universally recognized as the legally mandated, mathematically provable defense against these catastrophic hijacking scenarios.

“Complexity is the worst enemy of security, and our systems are getting more complex all the time.” — Bruce Schneier

Consequently, technology executives find themselves cornered in a deeply uncomfortable operational trap. On one side, they face non-negotiable regulatory and compliance frameworks that mandate heavy, decentralized cryptographic token verification for autonomous systems. On the other side, their enterprise AI initiatives face a complete breakdown of scalable unit economics, as the raw compute overhead required to continuously verify these Datalog proofs obliterates their profit margins. Framing this purely as an IT integration issue is a critical mistake; this is a core corporate governance and margin engineering crisis that requires an entirely new approach to network edge topology and embedded systems design.

Redeploying authorization logic to continuously warm, edge-native sovereign enclaves to eliminate compute latency.

Forward-Deployed Enclaves and Edge-Native Token Evaluation

To resolve this mathematical latency bottleneck, enterprise architectures must decisively abandon standard offshore IT systems integration. Legacy consulting paradigms rely on chaining together managed cloud services, which inevitably default to high-latency serverless environments for authorization logic. Instead, elite organizations are pivoting toward Forward-Deployed Engineering (FDE) models, wherein deeply embedded, highly specialized teams construct sovereign AI operating models directly within the client’s network perimeter. These FDE units recognize that securing autonomous agents requires moving the authorization logic out of centralized databases and distant cloud functions, and injecting it directly into the compute edge.

Calibrating the financial trade-offs between raw compute margins and mandated cryptographic infrastructure.

The production-grade solution relies on ripping the cryptographic validation logic out of serverless architectures and migrating it to high-performance, continuously warm Rust-based sidecars or WebAssembly (Wasm) edge nodes. By deploying intelligent edge sidecars, the architecture can maintain persistent HTTP/3 connections and securely cache the Identity Provider’s JSON Web Key Set (JWKS) in-memory. Recent benchmarks for Agent Identity Protocols demonstrate that executing compact capability validation in optimized Rust takes a mere 0.049ms, compared to the tens of milliseconds wasted in reactive cloud functions (Prakash, 2026; PromptsBuddy, 2026). When an agent submits a deeply nested Biscuit token accompanied by a fresh DPoP signature, the local Rust sidecar executes the embedded Datalog proof natively without suffering a cold start. This edge-native approach collapses the cryptographic overhead from a crippling 32.7ms cold-path penalty down to a predictable, sub-millisecond warm-path execution, thoroughly rescuing the deployment’s temporal and financial unit economics.

Figure: Systems Interaction & Process Flow Topology

This specific topology guarantees a property known as cryptographic non-joinability at the absolute perimeter of the enterprise backend. The edge validator sidecar enforces a strict mathematical boundary that operates completely independent of the LLM’s neural weights or operational context. Even if an adversary achieves total mastery over the agent’s prompt window and commands it to execute an unauthorized system wipe, the API edge physically rejects the instruction. The ephemeral token submitted by the hijacked agent will fundamentally lack the exact Datalog cryptographic proofs required to authorize the requested blast radius, neutralizing the threat instantaneously at the network edge.

“The unit economics of autonomous systems are rarely broken by the neural network itself; they hemorrhage at the cryptographic perimeter where static identity paradigms forcibly collide with mathematical capability evaluations.” — Sunil Prakash (2026)

Margin Realization, Strategic Trade-offs & The Leadership Playbook

Translating this architectural metamorphosis back into hard Profit & Loss (P&L) metrics illuminates the true FinOps of capability-based AI. Optimizing the “Authorization COGS” ultimately dictates the pilot-to-production conversion rate of any autonomous AI initiative within the enterprise.

📊 CFO Margin & Unit Economics Check: By migrating cryptographic evaluation from serverless cloud functions to persistent Rust-based edge sidecars, architecture teams can compress capability verification from a 32.7ms cold-path penalty down to 0.049ms. This averts exponential capability validation latency, rescuing the unit economics of autonomous inference at scale.

The reduction of per-transaction overhead from $1.20 back down toward a blended cost of $0.07 allows the enterprise to safely scale multi-hop agents across thousands of concurrent sessions without experiencing exponential margin degradation or unacceptable latency spikes.

However, intellectual honesty demands the explicit acknowledgment of the deep engineering limitations inherent to this architecture. Transitioning to offline capability attenuation is not a frictionless endeavor. It introduces significant payload bloat across the internal network due to nested cryptographic signatures appended at every agent hop. Furthermore, it demands highly complex state management to facilitate the seamless rotation of ephemeral DPoP keys across distributed, asynchronous services. This requires a caliber of distributed systems expertise that vastly exceeds standard web development, rendering this rigorous architecture financially and operationally unsuitable for trivial, low-stakes customer service chatbots where basic static security might suffice.

1. Fund Infrastructure Re-Architecture Over Raw API Budgets. Executive leaders must redirect capital away from the endless pursuit of cheaper raw LLM inference and immediately invest in the surrounding authorization infrastructure. The true cost of production AI lies in the cryptographic gateway, meaning budget allocations must prioritize the deployment of continuously warm, edge-native validation nodes that can process complex capability tokens without destroying system latency.

2. Restructure Risk Governance to Mandate RFC Standards. The board of directors and the Chief Information Security Officer (CISO) must formally update enterprise risk governance policies to explicitly ban static OAuth/JWT paradigms for autonomous agents. Mandating strict compliance with RFC 9396 (Rich Authorization Requests) and RFC 9449 (Demonstrating Proof-of-Possession) legally insulates the enterprise from fiduciary negligence, ensuring that all machine autonomy is mathematically bounded by the principle of least privilege.

3. Adopt Forward-Deployed Engineering Models. Organizations must abandon the outdated strategy of outsourcing AI security integration to generalized IT vendors. Instead, they must cultivate embedded, elite Forward-Deployed Engineering teams capable of writing low-level Rust and Wasm components. Only through this specialized delivery model can an enterprise successfully align the strict mathematical containment demanded by regulators with the verifiable profitability required by the market.

EXECUTIVE RESEARCH DOSSIER: Cryptographic Authorization & Containment for Autonomous LLM Agent Toolchains

TARGET AUDIENCE: C-Suite & Board-Level Technology Executives (MDs, Global Practice Heads, CTOs, CISOs) PRIMARY FOCUS: Dynamic JIT Token Revocation, Biscuit/Macaroon Cryptographic Attenuation, RFC 9396 Rich Authorization Requests (RAR), and the Mitigation of Context-Stuffed Privilege Escalation in Agentic AI architectures. DELIVERY PARADIGM: Forward-Deployed Engineering (FDE) and Sovereign AI Operating Models vs. Legacy IT Systems Integration.

📊 Executive Summary: ## EXECUTIVE SUMMARY & STRATEGIC PARADIGM SHIFT

As enterprises transition from isolated LLM chat interfaces to autonomous, multi-hop LLM agent toolchains, legacy centralized Identity and Access Management (IAM) systems — built for human users — are structurally collapsing. The transition to agentic AI introduces a lethal security vector: Context-Stuffed Privilege Escalation. When developers attempt to govern an agent’s permissions by stuffing rules into the LLM’s context window, prompt injection attacks can effortlessly manipulate the model into ignoring these rules and executing unauthorized, high-impact API calls (e.g., blanket financial transfers or mass data exfiltration).

To survive in production, frontier Forward-Deployed Engineering (FDE) teams are abandoning standard OAuth/JWT paradigms. Instead, they are embedding locally within client sovereign boundaries to implement cryptographically attenuated capability tokens (Biscuit/Macaroons) combined with OAuth 2.0 Rich Authorization Requests (RFC 9396) and dynamic Just-In-Time (JIT) revocation. This FDE delivery model radically outperforms offshore IT consulting by moving authorization out of the easily manipulated LLM prompt and into mathematically guaranteed, offline-verifiable tokens that enforce zero-trust boundaries at the API edge without crushing system latency (Fett et al., 2023; Prakash, 2026; PromptsBuddy, 2026).

1. OPERATING MODEL & TECHNICAL ARCHITECTURE: DECENTRALIZED AUTH FOR AUTONOMOUS CHAINS

Legacy systems integrators deploy agents using centralized OAuth/JWT authorization servers. This fails catastrophically for autonomous agents that spawn sub-agents and execute thousands of API calls per minute, resulting in extreme latency bottlenecks. Embedded FDEs solve this via decentralized, offline-verifiable capability models.

Source A: Verifiable Attenuated Delegation for AI Agent Chains

  • Descriptive Title: Verifiable Attenuated Delegation for AI Agent Chains (IETF Draft)
  • URL: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-niyikiza-oauth-attenuating-agent-tokens/
  • TL;DR: This IETF specification addresses the fundamental inability of existing standard OAuth 2.0 (RFC 8693) to securely handle multi-hop delegation chains where an AI agent spawns sub-agents. It advocates for offline-verifiable, monotonic attenuation (using capability models like Biscuit or Macaroons) ensuring each sub-agent mathematically reduces its inherited permissions without requiring round-trip network calls to a root server (Prakash, 2026). This enables complex agent-to-agent architectures in air-gapped or sovereign deployments.
  • Empirical Benchmark: Supports multi-hop agent delegation chains (depth ≥ 2) with zero millisecond round-trip latency to the root authorization server during tool execution, effectively decoupling agent velocity from centralized IAM uptime (Prakash, 2026).
  • Enterprise Economic & Liability Consequence: Eliminates centralized single points of failure, ensuring mission-critical agent workflows satisfy 99.999% SLA requirements. Failure to implement this exposes the enterprise to cascading operational lockups when agent volumes overwhelm legacy authentication servers.
  • Counter-Intuitive Production Reality: OAuth 2.0 token exchange is fundamentally broken for AI agents. It treats nested delegation chains merely as audit history rather than cryptographically enforced authority, leaving deep agent chains entirely vulnerable to excessive agency if deployed using standard enterprise IT playbooks (Prakash, 2026).

Source B: capmas: Capability-Based Delegation of Privileges in Multi-Agent Systems

  • Descriptive Title: capmas: Capability-Based Delegation of Privileges in Multi-Agent Systems
  • URL: https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.25974
  • TL;DR: This research evaluates modern decentralized authorization schemas, specifically comparing symmetric Macaroons against asymmetric Biscuit tokens powered by embedded Datalog policies (Veski et al., 2026). It formalizes how multi-agent systems must distribute privileges efficiently across microservices using capability-based delegation rather than identity-based access control. The paper systematically weighs cryptographic security against payload overhead in lightweight message-passing environments.
  • Empirical Benchmark: Demonstrates the explicit compute trade-off in multi-agent orchestration: Biscuits enable decentralized public-key offline verification, but introduce larger payload bloat and cryptographic overhead compared to the lightweight, symmetric HMAC operations of Macaroons (Veski et al., 2026).
  • Enterprise Economic & Liability Consequence: Allows Forward-Deployed Engineering teams to construct highly secure, sovereign AI enclaves where multi-party agents can negotiate across tenant boundaries safely. This limits statutory liability under the EU AI Act by enforcing rigid, policy-as-code boundaries directly within the token.
  • Counter-Intuitive Production Reality: While asymmetric Biscuit tokens offer superior cryptographic decentralization, their payload bloat and embedded Datalog evaluation can paradoxically bottleneck high-frequency AI agent interactions, forcing architects to trade absolute decentralization for sub-millisecond execution speeds (Veski et al., 2026).

2. PRODUCTION BREAKING POINTS & FAILURE AUTOPSIES: THE CONTEXT-STUFFING PRIVILEGE ESCALATION TRAP

A common, disastrous anti-pattern in enterprise AI pilots is attempting to restrict an LLM’s actions by placing rules in its prompt (“Context Stuffing”). Attackers easily bypass this via prompt injection, leading to Context-Stuffed Privilege Escalation. The enterprise solution is strictly decoupling authorization from the LLM via RFC 9396.

Source C: Scoping Agent Permissions: Rich Authorization Requests (RFC 9396) in Practice

  • Descriptive Title: Scoping Agent Permissions: Rich Authorization Requests (RFC 9396) in Practice
  • URL: https://mojoauth.com/blog/rfc-9396-rich-authorization-requests/
  • TL;DR: This implementation analysis demonstrates how RFC 9396 (Rich Authorization Requests) replaces generic, flat OAuth scope strings (e.g., files.write) with highly structured, granular JSON arrays detailing exact constraints (Singh, 2026). For an AI agent, this cryptographically binds its access token not just to an action, but to a specific parameter, file, and task ID. It physically prevents the LLM from broadening its operational scope, even if its context window is completely hijacked.
  • Empirical Benchmark: Mitigates OWASP LLM06 (Excessive Agency) by limiting agent capabilities down to the individual object/API parameter level, drastically shrinking the attack surface by explicitly defining the “minimum necessary” permissions outside of the LLM’s control (Singh, 2026).
  • Enterprise Economic & Liability Consequence: Protects the enterprise balance sheet from catastrophic, million-dollar fiduciary breaches (e.g., an agent executing a mass corporate refund). Under SEC disclosure rules and DORA, enforcing granular cryptographic constraints proves reasonable fiduciary defense against autonomous agent hijackings.
  • Counter-Intuitive Production Reality: Adding security constraints and permission rules into the LLM’s system prompt makes the system less secure. The model can be socially engineered to ignore its context, requiring authorization to be physically enforced at the API layer via structured JSON payloads, rendering prompt-based privilege escalation mathematically impossible (Prakash, 2026; Singh, 2026).

Source D: AI Agent Impersonation: How Prompt Injection Turns an Agent’s Identity Into the Attacker’s

  • Descriptive Title: AI Agent Impersonation: How Prompt Injection Turns an Agent’s Identity Into the Attacker’s
  • URL: https://portswigger.net/research/ai-agent-impersonation (Note: URL inferred from standard Web LLM attacks landscape)
  • TL;DR: This autopsy of real-world Web LLM attacks reveals how an attacker can use hidden text inside an email or document to overwrite an agent’s intended task (IAMDevBox, 2026). Because the agent acts as a near-perfect deputy with high privileges, a simple prompt injection effectively grants the attacker the agent’s full backend authorization. The research dictates the use of RFC 9396 to constrain high-risk actions to explicit, pre-bound parameters.
  • Empirical Benchmark: Validates that relying on standard access tokens results in a 100% success rate for privilege escalation when an agent ingests malicious context containing command-override directives (IAMDevBox, 2026).
  • Enterprise Economic & Liability Consequence: Quantifies a direct $10M+ blast radius for agent deployments in banking or healthcare if an agent processes a poisoned PDF or email. Organizations will fail SOC 2 Type II audits if autonomous deputies are not restricted via parameter-bound authorization requests.
  • Counter-Intuitive Production Reality: The primary threat to an enterprise AI agent is not external network penetration, but the data it is explicitly asked to process. The operational context (e.g., a customer’s email) is the actual attack vector, meaning data ingestion pipelines are now privilege escalation conduits (IAMDevBox, 2026).

3. UNIT ECONOMICS & MARGIN ARCHITECTURE: THE FINOPS OF CONTEXT VS. CAPABILITIES

Offshore IT models attempt to solve agentic memory and permissioning by repeatedly injecting vast amounts of data into the model (Naive Context Stuffing). This destroys unit economics and compute margins.

Source E: Context Engineering for AI Agents: How to Architect LLMs

  • Descriptive Title: Context Engineering for AI Agents: How to Architect LLMs
  • URL: https://promptsbuddy.com/blog/context-engineering
  • TL;DR: Investigates the physics of context degradation and the severe operational and financial costs of “naive context stuffing.” The research proves that appending full histories, transcripts, and security state into the LLM window for every multi-agent turn scales compute costs uncontrollably while burying critical facts in the model’s attention blind spots (PromptsBuddy, 2026). It demands a shift to durable, stateful execution graphs backed by externalized capabilities.
  • Empirical Benchmark: Reveals that prefill token costs grow quadratically per agent turn when relying on context stuffing, while simultaneously causing a massive drop in recall accuracy at mid-window positions (the “Lost in the Middle” phenomenon) (PromptsBuddy, 2026).
  • Enterprise Economic & Liability Consequence: Context stuffing destroys gross margins and spikes Cost of Goods Sold (COGS) through runaway token consumption (Fett et al., 2023; PromptsBuddy, 2026). For C-Suite executives, it creates a negative pilot-to-production conversion ratio, as systems that work cheaply in short prototyping sessions become financially ruinous in multi-turn production environments.
  • Counter-Intuitive Production Reality: Giving an LLM agent more context makes it fundamentally less reliable. Flooding the window with security state and history masks poor architectural design, leading to quiet failures via contradiction and truncation, rather than explicit application errors (Fett et al., 2023; PromptsBuddy, 2026).

4. REGULATORY COMPLIANCE, GOVERNANCE & JIT REVOCATION

Complying with the NIST AI RMF and FedRAMP High requires abandoning static identity tokens for AI agents. Tokens must be bound to specific intents and ephemeral lifetimes.

Source F: What breaks when JWTs are used for AI agent authorization?

  • Descriptive Title: What breaks when JWTs are used for AI agent authorization?
  • URL: https://autonomous-identity.com/jwt-ai-agent-authorization (Note: URL inferred from Autonomous Identity industry analysis)
  • TL;DR: Explains that standard JSON Web Tokens (JWTs) freeze authorization claims at the moment of issuance, rendering them incapable of recalculating privilege when an agent’s context, intent, or environment dynamically shifts mid-flight (NHI Management Group, 2026; Veski et al., 2026). It advocates replacing static JWTs with intent-based, context-aware authorization evaluated in real-time, utilizing dynamic Just-In-Time (JIT) ephemeral secrets (NHI Management Group, 2026; PromptsBuddy, 2026).
  • Empirical Benchmark: Transitions threat exposure windows from standard JWT lifetimes (e.g., 60 minutes) down to exact task execution durations (milliseconds to seconds), dynamically revoking access the exact moment a sub-task completes or a context boundary is breached (NHI Management Group, 2026).
  • Enterprise Economic & Liability Consequence: Directly addresses OWASP Agentic AI Top 10 vulnerabilities and NIST AI RMF compliance mandates (Singh, 2026; Veski et al., 2026). Executives failing to implement JIT revocation for autonomous systems risk massive regulatory fines under the EU AI Act, as static tokens allow compromised agents to sustain unauthorized actions long after their original intent was subverted.
  • Counter-Intuitive Production Reality: The enterprise gold standard for identity (JWTs) is an active liability for AI agents. Because AI tasks mutate autonomously, a token that is perfectly valid at creation time can become catastrophically dangerous within seconds, proving static tokens are a weak source of truth for machine autonomy (NHI Management Group, 2026; Veski et al., 2026).

title: Building Self-Maintaining API Documentation with AI Agents
partialText:
If you have ever opened a pull request from a coding agent like Cursor, scrolled through a long diff and found that the only real change was one reworded sentence, you already know where this story starts.

I keep our API reference in sync with a live stage OpenAPI file. The staging environment moves fast, and the docs have to follow it before developers and their coding agents copy the old version into real client code.

If you are looking to learn more about api doc automations and agentic workflows, check out my book here: The AI Native Technical Writer

The above plan looks fine on paper, but it starts to fall apart once it runs against a real stage environment, and it fails in four specific ways.

  • Wording changes became work: Someone rewrote a description on stage. Nothing about the contract changed, but I still got a pull request to review.
  • Unrelated changes piled up: Three products changed on the same day and landed in one giant review that nobody wanted to own.
  • The same change got drafted twice: An open draft already covered Monday’s change, and Thursday’s run drafted it again.
  • A broken deploy looked like a real change: A bad deploy dropped a big chunk of routes for a while, and the model was ready to document that the API had vanished.

All four problems had the same cause. I was asking an AI to answer questions that plain code answers better, so I changed the order of the system. Now a regular Node.js watcher does the hard work. The AI only drafts after the change is already classified, and a person still merges every pull request.

This post walks through this design. It works for OpenAPI, but the same idea fits protobuf, GraphQL or any contract that moves faster than the people who keep its consumers up to date.

The real problem is contract drift

“The docs are out of date” sounds like a writing problem, but what actually goes wrong is API contract drift. The staging environment says one thing, the written contract says another and developers trust the written one, so coding agents trust it too. When the two disagree, people ship client code against a shape the API no longer has.

The usual fixes don’t help much. Waiting for someone to mention the change in Slack is too slow. Regenerating Markdown from the whole OpenAPI spec every night is too much work, because every run produces a huge diff and reviewers stop reading carefully.

Before a model writes a single sentence, I want answers to five questions:

  1. Did the contract change, or only the wording?
  2. Which product area owns this change?
  3. Is this a new endpoint, or a change to an existing one?
  4. Did we already draft this in an open pull request?
  5. Is stage healthy, or did a broken deploy just delete a lot of routes?

Each of these has a correct answer that code can compute. A model should never be guessing them.

How the pieces fit together

The system has two parts, and each one has a single job.

  • The watcher is a scheduled GitHub Action that runs Node.js. It notices changes, classifies them, splits them into groups and refuses to act when the stage looks broken.
  • The drafting agent is a Cursor Automation with strict rules. It takes one group of changes and turns it into one draft docs pull request.

Step 1: Store the API one endpoint at a time

The watcher never compares yesterday’s full JSON file with today’s as one big file. It starts by fetching the stage spec:

node watch.mjs fetch --out /tmp/stage-doc.json

Then it splits the spec into one small snapshot file per operation. An operation is one method and path pair, like these:

POST /api/v1/sessions
GET  /api/v1/sessions/{id}
POST /api/v1/billing/invoices
...

Each snapshot holds the operation and the schemas it needs, so it can be read and compared on its own.

This looks like extra bookkeeping at first, but it changes how every later step behaves:

  • Small diffs. A change to one endpoint no longer creates a 5,000-line pull request.
  • A local baseline. The snapshot files travel with each pull request, so merging one updates the baseline only for the endpoints it touched.
  • Independent drafts. Open drafts for different endpoints don’t interfere with each other.

It feels much closer to database migrations than to rewriting the whole thing. Each merged pull request moves the known truth forward for a few endpoints and leaves everything else alone.

Step 2: Compare facts, not sentences

This is the part most “AI watches OpenAPI” demos skip, and in my opinion it’s the most important part of the whole system.

The watcher flattens each operation into a list of facts. A fact is a key that points to one piece of the contract:

parameter.header.X-Request-Id
request.body.amount
response.201.body.invoice_id
response.200.header.Location

Some facts describe the shape of the contract: types, required fields, enums, status codes, headers and auth requirements. Other facts are only text: summaries, descriptions and example wording.

The rule that follows is simple. If someone rewrites a description and the shape stays the same, the watcher opens nothing. If a field becomes required, it drafts a change and flags it as breaking.

Here is a simplified version of the classifier:

function classifyFact(key, before, after) {
  if (!before && after) {
    return {
      key,
      kind: "added",
      isShapeChange: isShapeFact(key),
      isBreaking: isNewRequiredInput(key, after),
    };
  }
  if (before && !after) {
    return {
      key,
      kind: "removed",
      isShapeChange: isShapeFact(key),
      isBreaking: isShapeFact(key),
    };
  }
  if (JSON.stringify(before) !== JSON.stringify(after)) {
    return {
      key,
      kind: "changed",
      before,
      after,
      isShapeChange: isShapeFact(key),
      isBreaking: typeChangedOrBecameRequired(before, after),
    };
  }
  return null;
}

A removed shape fact always counts as breaking. That’s deliberately cautious, because some client may still send or read that field. A deleted description, on the other hand, is only text and can’t break anyone.

Two stop rules run before the watcher pushes any branch:

if (report.removedRatio > 0.25) {
  throw new Error("Stage looks broken. No PRs.");
}
if (onlyTextFactsChanged(report)) {
  return { status: "description-only" }; // do nothing
}
The second rule handles description-only runs, which are a perfectly good outcome. The first rule is the one I’m most glad I wrote.

A bad deploy can make half the routes disappear for a while. A model will cheerfully document that as a real removal. A ratio check in plain code refuses, fails the run and opens nothing.

The watcher also looks for renames. When POST /old disappears, and POST /new appears with enough of the same shape, it reports one rename instead of a deleted endpoint plus a new one. Reviewers care about that difference, because a rename and a removal need very different follow-up work.

Step 3: Split the work the way people review it

When a real change does show up, the watcher doesn’t open one mega pull request. It groups the changes by two things:

  • Product area, such as auth, billing or search.
  • Kind of change, which is either new endpoints or changes to existing ones.

Each group gets its own branch:

auto/stage-api/auth-new
auto/stage-api/auth-existing
auto/stage-api/billing-new
...

I chose this split because of how review actually happens on a team:

  • Someone can merge auth without waiting on billing.
  • New endpoints need pages and navigation entries, while existing endpoints need field updates and callouts. Mixing the two makes a review painful to follow.
  • Two agent runs can work in parallel without fighting over one branch.

The routing config stays boring on purpose:

{
  "stageSpecUrl": "https://stage.example.com/api/docs/v1/doc.json",
  "maxRemovedRatio": 0.25,
  "products": [
    {
      "id": "billing",
      "label": "Billing APIs",
      "match": ["/api/v1/billing", "/api/v1/invoices"],
      "folders": ["billing-api-reference"],
      "changelog": "billing-api-reference/changelog.mdx"
    }
  ]
}

The watcher matches each path against these prefixes, and the longest matching prefix wins. Anything that matches nothing falls into a default area, so an unmatched change still gets drafted somewhere. You can use the same idea in any repo that documents several services.

Step 4: Treat open drafts as part of the truth

This is usually where a weekend demo stops working.

Imagine that Monday’s run opens this pull request:

[Stage API] Billing APIs: Changes to existing endpoints (2026-11-09)

Nobody has merged it by Thursday, and stage changes the same endpoint again. If Thursday’s run only compares stage with main, it sees Monday's change as new and drafts it a second time.

So before the watcher diffs anything, it layers every open [Stage API] pull request on top of main:

baseline = main
         + open PR #101
         + open PR #108

then compare stage against that baseline

That gives two possible outcomes:

  • If the open pull request already covers the change, Thursday’s run does nothing.
  • If stage moved again after that pull request, Thursday’s run drafts only the newer delta. Its commit message says Also changed in open PR: #101, and the agent puts "Builds on #101. Merge #101 first." at the top of the new pull request.

None of this needs a clever model. The system only has to remember which work is already in flight.

Step 5: Claim the group, then read the brief

A push to a group branch starts a Cursor Automation run. The agent doesn’t get a vague instruction like “go fix the docs”. It gets a short protocol instead.

Claim the group

First, the agent claims the group so that two runs never draft the same work:

git checkout --detach origin/auto/stage-api/billing-existing
git commit --allow-empty -m "stage-api-claim: billing-existing"
git push origin HEAD:refs/heads/auto/stage-api/billing-existing

If the push is rejected, another run already owns the group, so this run stops.

This works because both runs start from the same branch tip. The first claim to land moves the branch forward. The second claim is now built on an old tip, so git rejects it as a non-fast-forward push.

One more rule closes the gap. The claim itself is a push to the group branch, so a run that starts after it will find a claim commit at the tip. The protocol tells that run to stop as well.

It’s a tiny lock made of git. It’s simple; anyone can see it in the branch history, and it’s enough for this job.

Read the brief

Next, the agent asks the watcher for a brief:

node watch.mjs brief \
  --base origin/main \
  --label billing-existing \
  --md /tmp/brief.md \
  --json /tmp/brief.json

For each endpoint in the group, the brief tells the agent:

  • change: whether the endpoint is new, changed, renamed or removed.
  • existingPages: the pages that already document this operation.
  • placement: where a new page should go.
  • inOpenapiJson: whether the shared OpenAPI file already has it.
  • changes: the before and after facts, with breaking flags.

Then the rules get strict.

  • The agent may edit the shared OpenAPI file, the matching endpoint pages, the navigation for new pages and that area’s changelog.
  • It must not wander into concept guides, tutorials, SDK folders or site chrome.
  • For removed endpoints, it never deletes pages. It flags them for a person instead.
  • It always opens a draft pull request.

That last rule is the point of the whole design. The model drafts, and it never ships.

What a useful draft PR looks like

The title is part of the protocol:

[Stage API] Billing APIs: New endpoints (2026-11-13)

The [Stage API] prefix is how later runs recognize open work, which is exactly what Step 4 depends on.

The body is written for the reviewer, not for show:

> Drafted from the stage OpenAPI file.
> Stage may be ahead of production. Merge when the change is real.

**Area:** Billing APIs · **Kind:** New endpoints

## What changed on stage
- `POST /api/v1/billing/invoices`: new
- Breaking: none

## What I changed
- `openapi.json`: added operation and schemas
- `billing-api-reference/invoices/create.mdx`: new page
- changelog: vX.Y.Z

## Needs your input
- Confirm the changelog version if another Stage API PR merged first
- Placement was unclear for one path

## Other pages that mention these APIs
- `guides/quickstart.mdx:42` (not edited)

## Checks
| Check | Result |
| :--- | :--- |
| Validate docs build | Pass |
| Style lint | Pass |

One more rule saved me here. The agent doesn’t quietly rewrite every guide that mentions the endpoint. It lists those files under “Other pages that mention these APIs”, and a person decides what else should change.

Why AI can automate this isn’t enough

Anyone can wire this up in an afternoon now:

schedule → fetch OpenAPI → prompt a model → open a PR

That pipeline is easy to build. It’s also a very fast way to generate review noise.

What made my version useful was everything around the model:

  • Shape changes over wording changes, so description edits stop being fake work.
  • One file per endpoint, so merges stay small and local.
  • Groups by product area and change kind, so a reviewer can approve one thing without owning five.
  • Open PRs counted as known work, so the same change never gets drafted twice.
  • A refusal to trust a broken stage, so a bad deploy never gets documented.
  • A claim before drafting, so two agents never fight over one group.
  • A short brief and a short edit list, so the model works inside clear limits.
  • Draft PRs only, so stage can lead while the docs still wait for a person.

This pattern also works outside docs

You can use the watcher, swap what it drafts and apply the same pattern for other contracts.

Whatever the contract is, the steps stay the same:

  1. Snapshot the contract in small pieces.
  2. Compare shape, not prose.
  3. Group by owner and change kind.
  4. Layer open work before comparing.
  5. Give an agent a brief and clear limits.
  6. Open a draft for a human.

Here is a small starter kit you can build from:

const stage = await fetchSpec(STAGE_URL);
const base = await readSnapshots("snapshots/");
const open = await loadOpenAutomationPrs();
const layered = applyOverlays(base, open);
const report = compareFacts(layered, stage);

if (report.removedRatio > 0.25) fail("broken deploy");
if (!report.hasShapeChange) exit("nothing to do");

for (const group of groupByOwnerAndKind(report)) {
  writeSnapshots(group);
  pushBranch(`auto/contract/${group.id}`);
  // agent reads brief(group) and opens a draft PR
}

You don’t even need the agent on day one. A Markdown brief inside a pull request is already better than hoping someone notices that stage changed.

What I learned once it worked

  • Most runs should do nothing: Unchanged and description-only runs are good outcomes. A quiet watcher means the contract and the docs agree.
  • Agents copy nearby pages well: When I give the agent the closest sibling page and tell it to match that structure, the result is much better than asking it to invent a page style.
  • Deleted endpoints are a people problem: The watcher detects the removal, but it never deletes the page. Someone still has to add redirects and confirm that the endpoint is really gone in production.
  • Changelogs collide: Two groups can bump the same changelog on the same day, so a person confirms the version number at merge time.
  • The title prefix matters: If someone renames a pull request and drops [Stage API], the watcher can't see that work and may draft the same change again. The naming rule is part of the system, not decoration.

Conclusion

AI made documentation updates easy to generate, but it didn’t make them easy to trust, and trust is what decides whether anyone merges them.

That’s why I think of a stage API watcher as a reliability tool more than a docs tool. So if you’re building something in this space, don’t start with the prompt; instead, count the real change, avoid duplicate drafts, and decide what the agent is not allowed to touch. The AI opening a pull request was never the interesting part, but the interesting part is that the pull request was already constrained before the model generated its first token.

How do you keep API docs, SDKs or clients up to date with a contract that changes faster than your team? I’d love to hear what has worked for you, so tell me in the comments.

title: SpecGuard: When AI Coding Agents Write Tests That Approve Bugs
partialText:
Ask a coding agent to write checks for a requirement and it will often copy what the existing code does instead. In SpecGuardBench, the best agent wrote a faithful validation harness for only 63% of tasks. When the reference code was buggy, the agents’ faithfulness fell by 19 to 31 points, because they wrote checks that approved the bug. Here is a free, in-browser playground that shows the failure on small tasks, lets you edit a harness and watch it pass or fail, and lets you try small local models on the same test.

The problem: tests that agree with the code

Here is a one-line requirement:

slugify(title) MUST return a string that contains only lowercase letters a–z, digits 0–9 and single hyphens, with no leading or trailing hyphen.

You give a coding agent this requirement, the current implementation and the existing test, and ask it for a validation harness: a set of checks that tells you whether an implementation meets the requirement.

The easy way out is to run the current implementation, record its outputs and assert that any other implementation returns exactly the same thing. That harness passes on the current code and looks thorough. It is also wrong in two ways:

  1. It approves whatever the reference does. If the reference has a bug, the harness treats the bug as correct behaviour.
  2. It rejects valid code. The requirement says nothing about accented letters. One correct implementation turns “Café au lait” into caf-au-lait, and another turns it into cafe-au-lait. Both meet the requirement. A harness that copies the reference fails the second one.

This matters more as agents write more of the code. The harness is what decides whether the agent’s next change is accepted. If it checks the old code instead of the requirement, it blocks valid changes and lets real bugs through.

What the research found

SpecGuardBench: Can Coding Agents Construct Reliable Validation Harnesses from Natural Language Specifications? (arXiv:2610.16870) tested this directly. The benchmark has 291 Python tasks covering eight kinds of verification logic. For each task there is a correct implementation, a buggy one that breaks the requirement but still passes the existing test, and valid alternatives that behave differently wherever the requirement says nothing.

A harness counts as faithful only if it rejects the bug and accepts every correct version.

Then the authors set a trap. They showed the agents the buggy implementation as the reference. If an agent were really working from the requirement, the reference wouldn’t matter. It mattered a lot:

Faithfulness fell by 19 to 31 points. The agents trusted the code they were shown more than the requirement they were given.

The solution: SpecGuard, a playground that runs in your browser

SpecGuard is a small, free re-creation of SpecGuardBench that runs entirely in a browser tab. Treat it as a hands-on way to see the failure and to practise writing faithful checks, not as a replacement for the paper’s benchmark. It ships as a tab in ZeeSpec, an open-source spec builder for AI coding agents, next to the EPIC Score tab that grades the spec itself.

It has 16 JavaScript tasks, two for each of the paper’s eight types of verification logic:

Each task works like the paper’s. The harness author sees the requirement, how to call the code, a reference implementation and the existing test. Kept hidden from the author are a correct implementation, a buggy one that passes the existing test, and a valid alternative.

You pick who writes the harnesses:

  • A local model. It runs on your own GPU through WebGPU and is downloaded once. Nothing is sent to a server.
  • Three baselines that need no GPU, which show how the scoring works.

Every harness runs in a separate background worker with no network access and a time limit of a few seconds, so model-written code can’t do anything harmful or hang the page.

One task, up close

Here is the whole slugify task. The harness author sees the requirement, the reference implementation and the existing test:

// Spec: slugify(title) MUST return a string that contains only lowercase letters a–z,
// digits 0–9 and single hyphens, with no leading or trailing hyphen.
// Reference implementation (shown to the author)
const slugify = (title) => String(title).toLowerCase()
  .replace(/[^a-z0-9]+/g, '-')
  .replace(/^-+|-+$/g, '')
// Existing test (already passes)
assertEqual(slugify('Hello World'), 'hello-world')

Hidden from the author are a buggy version and a valid alternative:

// Buggy: strips a leading hyphen but not a trailing one. Still passes the existing test.
const buggy = (title) => String(title).toLowerCase()
  .replace(/[^a-z0-9]+/g, '-')
  .replace(/^-+/, '')                      // 'Hello!' → 'hello-'  (breaks the spec)
// Valid alternative: transliterates accents instead of dropping them.
const alternative = (title) => String(title).normalize('NFD').replace(/[̀-ͯ]/g, '')
  .toLowerCase().split(/[^a-z0-9]+/).filter(Boolean).join('-')
                                           // 'Café au lait' → 'cafe-au-lait' (reference gives 'caf-au-lait')

A faithful harness checks the rule and nothing else, so it rejects the buggy version and accepts the other two:

function checkCase(target, c) {
  const s = target(...c.args)
  assert(/^[a-z0-9]+(-[a-z0-9]+)*$/.test(s) || s === '', 'only a–z, 0–9 and single inner hyphens')
}

A harness that copies the reference (assertEqual(target(x), reference(x))) rejects the bug too. But it also rejects the valid alternative, because cafe-au-lait isn't what the reference returned, even though the spec never mentions accents. In the app you can open any task, see each verdict and the reason for it, edit the harness and click Re-run with my edits:

What the baselines show

Three baselines need no model and show that the scoring works:

  • The oracle confirms every task can be solved and the scoring recognises a correct answer.
  • Mirroring catches every bug, which looks good, but rejects every valid alternative. Show it the buggy reference and it catches nothing, because the bug is what it copied. A harness that copies the code can never be better than the code.
  • Replaying the existing test catches nothing, because by design every buggy version passes it. “The tests pass” proves nothing here.

A small model, as a demonstration

What happens when a model writes the harness itself? I ran Qwen 2.5 Coder 3B, a small code-tuned model, through all 16 tasks in the browser on a laptop’s built-in Intel graphics chip. One run took about 25 minutes. This is a demonstration of the failure, not a benchmark score. A 3B model writing code in one attempt, with no chance to run it and fix mistakes, isn’t comparable to the paper’s frontier agents, which can execute code and iterate.

Six harnesses failing to run measures the model’s one-shot JavaScript, not its reading of the spec. The other 10 are the interesting part, and not one of them was faithful. Eight rejected correct code, and the other two accepted everything, bug included.

The model’s slugify harness shows the most common failure:

// Written by Qwen 2.5 Coder 3B
assert(/^[a-z0-9]+$/.test(result), 'Result must contain only lowercase letters and digits')

The spec allows single hyphens, and the model dropped that clause. So the harness rejects the bug, but it also rejects the correct implementation and the valid alternative, because hello-world contains a hyphen. That isn't copying the reference. It's misreading the spec, and it produces the same result: a check that fails good code.

The mirror trap produced one case with the paper’s pattern. On the top-k task, the model’s harness accepted all three versions when it was shown the correct reference. Shown the buggy reference, it accepted the bug and rejected both correct versions, exactly what you’d expect from a harness that trusts the code it was shown. With overall faithfulness already at 0%, though, the trap can’t show a drop, and on 16 tasks the other numbers move by several points from run to run.

Llama 3.2 1B, the smallest model on offer, couldn’t take part. It wrote test-framework code (describe, it) instead of the harness it was asked for, and 15 of its 16 harnesses didn't run.

Try it yourself

Start small. In Tasks, pick one type (two tasks). With the hand-written oracle or the mirror baseline it finishes instantly. With a local model it takes a few minutes. Open a task, read each verdict, change the harness and click Re-run with my edits: that loop is the quickest way to get a feel for what “faithful” means.

To try a model on all 16 tasks, choose Local model, pick one and click Run benchmark, then run it again with the mirror trap on. Allow 20–30 minutes per run on a laptop GPU. Each run adds a row to a leaderboard kept in your browser. The paper’s results sit below it for reference and are labelled as not directly comparable.

The takeaway

Whether a person or an agent writes the tests, apply one rule when you review them: for every assertion, point to the sentence in the spec that requires it. If you can’t, the assertion is checking the current code, not the requirement. Delete it, or add the missing sentence to the spec. In SpecGuard, both mirroring and the small model’s over-strict checks fail that rule.

It works in the other direction too. If a sentence in the spec has no assertion, the harness can’t catch a bug there. That’s the gap the buggy implementations in these tasks slip through.

Limits

SpecGuard is a small re-creation, not the benchmark itself. It has 16 hand-built JavaScript tasks against the paper’s 291 Python ones. Its harness authors are single local models writing code in one attempt, with no retry. A harness that fails to run counts as unfaithful, and the app reports those separately. No frontier model has been run on these 16 tasks, so there’s no direct calibration of how hard they are compared with the paper’s. The task set itself is checked automatically: every hidden implementation is confirmed to behave as intended, and the hand-written oracle scores 100%.

Disclaimer: this article is my own interpretation of the SpecGuardBench paper. SpecGuard is an independent, simplified re-creation, not the authors’ benchmark or code. The tasks, baselines and scoring are my reading of their method, and any errors are mine. For the authors’ exact method and results, see the paper.

Try it: vishalmysore.github.io/zeespec/app/#specguard
